slides.title: 1. Indications for testing and treatment
paragraphs: Test only when a positive result would lead to treatment. Once active H. pylori infection is established, eradication is recommended, even when symptoms are absent. Do not use serology to diagnose active infection or document cure.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
1. Indications for testing and treatment Test only when a positive result would lead to treatment. Once active H. pylori infection is established, eradication is recommended, even when symptoms are absent. Do not use serology to diagnose active infection or document cure. Test and treat Context Current or previous peptic ulcer disease Including patients using NSAIDs or aspirin. Eradication reduces ulcer recurrence; some patients still require gastroprotection. Gastric MALT lymphoma, gastric atrophy or intestinal metaplasia, early gastric cancer resection Eradication is indicated but does not remove the need for appropriate GI surveillance or oncologic care. Uninvestigated dyspepsia Noninvasive test-and-treat is appropriate in selected adults younger than 60 without features that justify endoscopy; apply individualized cancer risk assessment. Unexplained iron deficiency anemia or ITP Consider testing after appropriate evaluation for other causes. Higher gastric cancer risk or adult household contact of an infected person ACG 2024 expands testing to selected high-risk groups, including first-degree family history of gastric cancer and adult household contacts. Routine universal screening of low-risk asymptomatic adults is not established. Do not postpone an indicated diagnostic endoscopy in favor of an isolated stool or breath test when alarm findings or cancer risk warrants biopsy. Deferral is reasonable during an acute competing illness, pregnancy when treatment can safely wait, or when severe interactions, intolerance, or inability to adhere make immediate eradication impractical. Document why and arrange follow-up. Permanent observation of confirmed infection is generally not recommended. Deferring treatment or discontinuing further eradication attempts Confirmed active infection: The ACG 2024 guideline recommends eradication for all patients with confirmed H. pylori infection. Lack of symptoms alone is not an indication for observation. Active infection not established: An isolated positive H. pylori IgG, particularly after previous therapy, does not establish current infection. Confirm with urea breath testing, stool antigen testing, or appropriate biopsy-based testing before prescribing antibiotics. Temporary deferral: Eradication may be postponed when an acute competing illness, pregnancy without an urgent indication, significant drug interactions, or inability to complete treatment makes immediate therapy inappropriate. Reassess after the limiting condition resolves. Repeated treatment failure: The AGA 2021 Clinical Practice Update (Best Practice Advice 9) recommends individualized discussion of additional eradication attempts, balancing benefits against adverse effects and repeated antibiotic exposure. Frailty, limited life expectancy, major intolerance, and absence of peptic ulcer disease or identifiable gastric cancer risk factors may favor withholding another empiric regimen. This is an expert-practice recommendation for refractory infection, not a routine alternative to initial treatment. Consider susceptibility-guided treatment before abandoning further attempts when feasible. References: ACG guideline 2024 ; AGA Clinical Practice Update 2021, Best Practice Advice 9 and 10 . Risks of untreated infection Infection commonly persists for decades and causes chronic active gastritis. Lifetime peptic ulcer risk among infected patients is often estimated near 10–20%, varying by population; only a minority develop gastric cancer (often cited around 1–3%, strongly dependent on regional and individual risk). H. pylori is a class I gastric carcinogen and a cause of gastric MALT lymphoma. Eradication reduces, but does not abolish, subsequent gastric cancer risk, especially once premalignant mucosal changes are present. Avoid applying population averages to an individual patient as a precise prediction.

slides.title: 2. Diagnostic testing and limitations
paragraphs: Use urea breath testing (UBT) or a validated monoclonal stool antigen test for most patients who do not need endoscopy. Gastric biopsies are appropriate when endoscopy is clinically indicated. Stool PCR may also provide clarithromycin resistance prediction.

Before UBT, stool antigen, or stool PCR: stop PPIs and vonoprazan for 14 days; avoid systemic antibiotics and bismuth for at least four weeks. Check the performing laboratory's additional instructions. H2 blockers or antacids can bridge acid symptoms, although some UBT laboratories request a short H2-blocker hold.

Gastric biopsies are appropriate when endoscopy is clinically indicated. Stool PCR may also provide clarithromycin resistance prediction. Before UBT, stool antigen, or stool PCR: stop PPIs and vonoprazan for 14 days; avoid systemic antibiotics and bismuth for at least four weeks. Check the performing laboratory's additional instructions. H2 blockers or antacids can bridge acid symptoms, although some UBT laboratories request a short H2-blocker hold. Test Best use False negatives and other pitfalls 13C UBT Initial diagnosis and test of cure PPIs, PCABs, antibiotics, bismuth, low organism burden; altered gastric anatomy can affect interpretation. Monoclonal stool antigen Initial diagnosis and test of cure Recent suppressive medications; performance depends on assay. Prefer laboratory monoclonal tests over less-validated rapid tests. Gastric histology and rapid urease test When EGD is indicated; simultaneously evaluate mucosal disease Patchy colonization, gastric bleeding, atrophy, intestinal metaplasia, recent medications, inadequate antrum/body sampling. Negative biopsy does not always exclude infection. Serologic IgG Generally avoid in routine U.S. practice Antibodies persist after eradication. A positive result is not evidence of current infection and cannot serve as test of cure. 3. Initial treatment For treatment-naive adults with unknown susceptibility, the 2024 ACG guideline recommends optimized bismuth quadruple therapy for 14 days. Omeprazole-amoxicillin-rifabutin (Talicia) and vonoprazan-amoxicillin (Voquezna Dual Pak) are alternatives for patients without penicillin allergy. Regimen and brand Adult prescription Use Optimized bismuth quadruple, individual prescriptions (14 days) Packaged alternative: Pylera + separately prescribed PPI; see duration and dose differences below. Helidac is another bismuth-based co-pack. Standard-dose PPI BID; bismuth subcitrate 120–300 mg QID or subsalicylate 300–524 mg QID; tetracycline 500 mg QID; metronidazole 500 mg TID or QID Preferred empiric first-line and preferred salvage if never previously given in optimized form. Do not routinely substitute doxycycline for tetracycline. Omeprazole + amoxicillin + rifabutin (14 days) Packaged brand: Talicia (4 capsules TID). Omeprazole 40 mg TID + amoxicillin 1 g TID + rifabutin 50 mg TID Alternative empiric first-line; important empiric salvage after optimized BQT. Check drug interactions, CBC, rifamycin exposure. Vonoprazan + amoxicillin (14 days) Packaged brand: Voquezna Dual Pak. Vonoprazan 20 mg BID + amoxicillin 1 g TID Alternative first-line when no penicillin allergy; salvage evidence is less certain than its first-line evidence. Abbreviations. BID, twice daily; PPI, proton pump inhibitor; QID, four times daily; TID, three times daily. Pylera contains bismuth subcitrate potassium, metronidazole, and tetracycline, with a separately prescribed PPI. Its U.S. label describes a 10-day course; that is not identical in dose or duration to guideline-optimized 14-day bismuth quadruple therapy. See the commercial formulations reference for capsule counts. Clarithromycin combinations, including Voquezna Triple Pak, should only be used when clarithromycin susceptibility is demonstrated. Levofloxacin combinations are susceptibility-directed salvage options. Both appear in the fellow section rather than the empiric initial-treatment table. Assess adherence, drug interactions, renal function, and the feasibility of multiple daily doses before choosing a regimen. Prior macrolide or fluoroquinolone exposure increases concern for resistance even when prescribed for an unrelated indication. Lack of exposure does not establish susceptibility.

slides.title: 4. Test of cure
paragraphs: Perform UBT or laboratory-based stool antigen testing at least four weeks after the last antibiotic dose; hold PPIs and vonoprazan two weeks, and antibiotics/bismuth four weeks before testing. Biopsy-based testing can be used if EGD is otherwise necessary. Symptom improvement is not proof of eradication, and serology cannot confirm cure.

Positive test of cure after an adequately timed, properly performed test generally indicates persistent infection. When the last pre-treatment eradication was never documented, call this persistent infection or recrudescence rather than proven reinfection.

slides.title: Deferring treatment or discontinuing further eradication attempts
paragraphs: Confirmed active infection: The ACG 2024 guideline recommends eradication for all patients with confirmed H. pylori infection. Lack of symptoms alone is not an indication for observation.

Active infection not established: An isolated positive H. pylori IgG, particularly after previous therapy, does not establish current infection. Confirm with urea breath testing, stool antigen testing, or appropriate biopsy-based testing before prescribing antibiotics.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
1. Indications for testing and treatment Test only when a positive result would lead to treatment. Once active H. pylori infection is established, eradication is recommended, even when symptoms are absent. Do not use serology to diagnose active infection or document cure. Test and treat Context Current or previous peptic ulcer disease Including patients using NSAIDs or aspirin. Eradication reduces ulcer recurrence; some patients still require gastroprotection. Gastric MALT lymphoma, gastric atrophy or intestinal metaplasia, early gastric cancer resection Eradication is indicated but does not remove the need for appropriate GI surveillance or oncologic care. Uninvestigated dyspepsia Noninvasive test-and-treat is appropriate in selected adults younger than 60 without features that justify endoscopy; apply individualized cancer risk assessment. Unexplained iron deficiency anemia or ITP Consider testing after appropriate evaluation for other causes. Higher gastric cancer risk or adult household contact of an infected person ACG 2024 expands testing to selected high-risk groups, including first-degree family history of gastric cancer and adult household contacts. Routine universal screening of low-risk asymptomatic adults is not established. Do not postpone an indicated diagnostic endoscopy in favor of an isolated stool or breath test when alarm findings or cancer risk warrants biopsy. Deferral is reasonable during an acute competing illness, pregnancy when treatment can safely wait, or when severe interactions, intolerance, or inability to adhere make immediate eradication impractical. Document why and arrange follow-up. Permanent observation of confirmed infection is generally not recommended. Deferring treatment or discontinuing further eradication attempts Confirmed active infection: The ACG 2024 guideline recommends eradication for all patients with confirmed H. pylori infection. Lack of symptoms alone is not an indication for observation. Active infection not established: An isolated positive H. pylori IgG, particularly after previous therapy, does not establish current infection. Confirm with urea breath testing, stool antigen testing, or appropriate biopsy-based testing before prescribing antibiotics. Temporary deferral: Eradication may be postponed when an acute competing illness, pregnancy without an urgent indication, significant drug interactions, or inability to complete treatment makes immediate therapy inappropriate. Reassess after the limiting condition resolves. Repeated treatment failure: The AGA 2021 Clinical Practice Update (Best Practice Advice 9) recommends individualized discussion of additional eradication attempts, balancing benefits against adverse effects and repeated antibiotic exposure. Frailty, limited life expectancy, major intolerance, and absence of peptic ulcer disease or identifiable gastric cancer risk factors may favor withholding another empiric regimen. This is an expert-practice recommendation for refractory infection, not a routine alternative to initial treatment. Consider susceptibility-guided treatment before abandoning further attempts when feasible. References: ACG guideline 2024 ; AGA Clinical Practice Update 2021, Best Practice Advice 9 and 10 . Risks of untreated infection Infection commonly persists for decades and causes chronic active gastritis. Lifetime peptic ulcer risk among infected patients is often estimated near 10–20%, varying by population; only a minority develop gastric cancer (often cited around 1–3%, strongly dependent on regional and individual risk). H. pylori is a class I gastric carcinogen and a cause of gastric MALT lymphoma. Eradication reduces, but does not abolish, subsequent gastric cancer risk, especially once premalignant mucosal changes are present. Avoid applying population averages to an individual patient as a precise prediction.

paragraphs: Temporary deferral: Eradication may be postponed when an acute competing illness, pregnancy without an urgent indication, significant drug interactions, or inability to complete treatment makes immediate therapy inappropriate. Reassess after the limiting condition resolves.

Once active H. pylori infection is established, eradication is recommended, even when symptoms are absent. Do not use serology to diagnose active infection or document cure. Test and treat Context Current or previous peptic ulcer disease Including patients using NSAIDs or aspirin. Eradication reduces ulcer recurrence; some patients still require gastroprotection. Gastric MALT lymphoma, gastric atrophy or intestinal metaplasia, early gastric cancer resection Eradication is indicated but does not remove the need for appropriate GI surveillance or oncologic care. Uninvestigated dyspepsia Noninvasive test-and-treat is appropriate in selected adults younger than 60 without features that justify endoscopy; apply individualized cancer risk assessment. Unexplained iron deficiency anemia or ITP Consider testing after appropriate evaluation for other causes. Higher gastric cancer risk or adult household contact of an infected person ACG 2024 expands testing to selected high-risk groups, including first-degree family history of gastric cancer and adult household contacts. Routine universal screening of low-risk asymptomatic adults is not established. Do not postpone an indicated diagnostic endoscopy in favor of an isolated stool or breath test when alarm findings or cancer risk warrants biopsy. Deferral is reasonable during an acute competing illness, pregnancy when treatment can safely wait, or when severe interactions, intolerance, or inability to adhere make immediate eradication impractical. Document why and arrange follow-up. Permanent observation of confirmed infection is generally not recommended. Active infection not established: An isolated positive H. pylori IgG, particularly after previous therapy, does not establish current infection. Temporary deferral: Eradication may be postponed when an acute competing illness, pregnancy without an urgent indication, significant drug interactions, or inability to complete treatment makes immediate therapy inappropriate. Reassess after the limiting condition resolves. Repeated treatment failure: The AGA 2021 Clinical Practice Update (Best Practice Advice 9) recommends individualized discussion of additional eradication attempts, balancing benefits against adverse effects and repeated antibiotic exposure. This is an expert-practice recommendation for refractory infection, not a routine alternative to initial treatment. Consider susceptibility-guided treatment before abandoning further attempts when feasible. References: ACG guideline 2024 ; AGA Clinical Practice Update 2021, Best Practice Advice 9 and 10 . slides.title: 5. Management after treatment failure
paragraphs: Before prescribing salvage therapy, reconstruct each prior regimen (actual antibiotic, dose, frequency, days completed), dates, missed doses, PPI/PCAB use, previous macrolide or fluoroquinolone exposure, and exact timing of each diagnostic test.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
5. Management after treatment failure Before prescribing salvage therapy, reconstruct each prior regimen (actual antibiotic, dose, frequency, days completed), dates, missed doses, PPI/PCAB use, previous macrolide or fluoroquinolone exposure, and exact timing of each diagnostic test. Prior regimen Reasonable next step if susceptibility unknown Prior PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin, or an incomplete/nonoptimized regimen; no prior optimized bismuth therapy Omeprazole (or another standard-dose PPI) BID + bismuth QID + tetracycline 500 mg QID + metronidazole 500 mg TID/QID for 14 days. Packaged option: Pylera plus separate PPI, recognizing Pylera is labeled for 10 days and has different component doses. Completed optimized bismuth + tetracycline + metronidazole + PPI for 14 days without eradication Omeprazole 40 mg TID + amoxicillin 1 g TID + rifabutin 50 mg TID for 14 days; Talicia contains the same three drugs (4 capsules TID). The packaged product has limited direct salvage-trial evidence. Alternatively use susceptibility-directed therapy. Multiple failures or no usable empiric option Request molecular resistance testing and/or EGD with dedicated culture and susceptibility biopsies. Individualize salvage with GI, microbiology, and pharmacy. Documented clarithromycin or levofloxacin susceptibility Clarithromycin susceptible: vonoprazan 20 mg BID + amoxicillin 1 g BID + clarithromycin 500 mg BID (Voquezna Triple Pak), or PPI BID + amoxicillin 1 g BID + clarithromycin 500 mg BID, for 14 days. Levofloxacin susceptible: PPI BID + amoxicillin 1 g BID + levofloxacin 500 mg daily for 14 days. Account for prior antibiotics and contraindications. Abbreviations. BID, twice daily; BQT, bismuth quadruple therapy; EGD, esophagogastroduodenoscopy; PPI, proton pump inhibitor; QID, four times daily; TID, three times daily. Clarithromycin resistance commonly follows 23S rRNA mutations and predicts poor results with clarithromycin combinations. Fluoroquinolone resistance commonly follows gyrA alterations. Metronidazole resistance is more complex; higher-dose metronidazole with bismuth and adequate acid suppression can sometimes overcome in vitro resistance. Amoxicillin, tetracycline, and rifabutin resistance are generally less prevalent, but susceptibility patterns vary geographically.

slides.title: 7. Treatment considerations in special populations
rows: Optimized BQT is usually the principal empiric option. Formal allergy evaluation can restore effective amoxicillin-containing salvage options; do not assume every reported childhood reaction represents a persistent allergy.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
7. Treatment considerations in special populations Situation Practical change True immediate penicillin allergy Optimized BQT is usually the principal empiric option. Formal allergy evaluation can restore effective amoxicillin-containing salvage options; do not assume every reported childhood reaction represents a persistent allergy. CKD, especially severe impairment Reassess tetracycline, bismuth product, amoxicillin, and levofloxacin dosing/contraindications. Fixed packs may not allow adjustments. Check product labeling and pharmacy rather than extrapolate standard dosing. Pregnancy or breastfeeding Nonurgent eradication is commonly deferred; tetracycline, bismuth subsalicylate, and some other regimen components raise safety concerns. If ulcer bleeding or other urgent disease requires therapy, obtain specialist review. Prior severe antibiotic-associated colitis or C. difficile Discuss recurrence risk and stewardship tradeoffs. H. pylori therapy should not be withheld reflexively if eradication is indicated. Severe liver disease, cytopenias, interacting medications Check metronidazole dose in severe hepatic impairment, rifabutin interactions/myelotoxicity, and clarithromycin QT/CYP3A interactions. Baseline CBC may be appropriate for rifabutin in high-risk patients. Immunosuppressive therapy Check interactions, particularly rifamycins and clarithromycin with transplant/immunosuppressive drugs; immunosuppression itself does not establish a different eradication regimen.

slides.title: Approximate test accuracy and interpretation
paragraphs: Reported sensitivity and specificity vary by comparator, assay, population, and medication exposure. The following approximate ranges are not interchangeable with local laboratory validation data and mostly reflect appropriately performed tests in untreated adults.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Clinical reference Approximate test accuracy and interpretation Reported sensitivity and specificity vary by comparator, assay, population, and medication exposure. The following approximate ranges are not interchangeable with local laboratory validation data and mostly reflect appropriately performed tests in untreated adults. Modality Sensitivity Specificity Important caveat 13C UBT ~95–98% ~95–98% Device and validation dependent. Laboratory monoclonal stool antigen ~90–95% ~90–97% Lower with suppression, suboptimal rapid assays. Histopathology ~85–95% ~95–100% Sampling, staining, pathologist and bacterial density. Rapid urease biopsy ~85–95% ~95–100% Can lose sensitivity with bleeding or medications. Serology Highly assay-dependent Highly assay-dependent Even an analytically accurate IgG assay cannot distinguish past from active infection. Culture Variable, often below molecular methods Very high for organism identification Recovery heavily affected by transport and prior treatment. No single universal sensitivity/specificity should be assigned to stool PCR: use the specific assay validation and target. Ranges are educational approximations, not pooled head-to-head estimates. See diagnostic review and laboratory references below. Commercial combination products and pill burden Product Actual administration Caveats Pylera Bismuth subcitrate potassium + metronidazole + tetracycline Three capsules QID (after meals and at bedtime) plus a separately prescribed PPI BID. Each capsule: bismuth subcitrate potassium 140 mg, metronidazole 125 mg, tetracycline hydrochloride 125 mg. U.S. labeling is 10 days with omeprazole; the ACG 14-day optimized BQT recommendation should not be confused with package labeling. The Pylera schedule provides metronidazole 1.5 g/day and tetracycline 1.5 g/day, not the same component doses as individually prescribed optimized BQT. Talicia Omeprazole + amoxicillin + rifabutin Four capsules TID with food for 14 days (12 capsules/day); daily totals omeprazole 120 mg, amoxicillin 3 g, rifabutin 150 mg. Each capsule has omeprazole 10 mg, amoxicillin 250 mg, rifabutin 12.5 mg. Check renal impairment, rifamycin interactions and blood counts as indicated. Voquezna Dual Pak Vonoprazan + amoxicillin Vonoprazan 20 mg BID plus amoxicillin 1 g TID for 14 days. Confirm availability, kidney function and penicillin allergy; 14-day pack is designed for the dual regimen. Voquezna Triple Pak Vonoprazan + amoxicillin + clarithromycin Vonoprazan 20 mg BID, amoxicillin 1 g BID, clarithromycin 500 mg BID for 14 days. Only appropriate when clarithromycin susceptibility is documented under ACG recommendations, despite product marketing/label indications. Helidac is a co-pack containing bismuth subsalicylate, metronidazole, and tetracycline, taken with a separately prescribed acid suppressant. Follow current product instructions and verify commercial availability. Pylera is a fixed-combination capsule; its 10-day FDA labeling differs from the guideline's 14-day optimized bismuth regimen. Individual bismuth products have different salt and strength formulations. Confirm actual elemental/product strength and dosing with pharmacy. Metronidazole QID and tetracycline QID are a substantial adherence burden. Do not simply interchange Pylera and an optimized BQT prescription without checking doses and duration. Abbreviations. BID, twice daily; PPI, proton pump inhibitor; QID, four times daily; TID, three times daily. Adverse effects and medication counseling Bismuth can darken stool or tongue and may be unsuitable with salicylate hypersensitivity (subsalicylate formulation). Tetracycline interacts with polyvalent cations and is avoided in pregnancy; separate from calcium, iron and antacids as directed. Metronidazole causes nausea, metallic taste and neuropathy with prolonged exposure; assess warfarin interaction. Rifabutin can cause cytopenias, uveitis, discoloration of secretions, CYP interactions and resistance concerns when used for other mycobacterial indications. Amoxicillin requires allergy and renal assessment. Clarithromycin has QT, CYP3A, and drug-interaction concerns. Levofloxacin carries tendon, neuropathy, CNS, dysglycemia, aortic aneurysm risk and other FDA warnings; renal adjustment is required. Vonoprazan has drug interactions and renal/hepatic labeling considerations. Clinical cases Case 1. A patient took 14 days of BQT. A stool antigen assay is negative 8 days after finishing treatment while the patient is still taking pantoprazole. Answer: uninterpretable for cure; repeat after appropriate antibiotic/bismuth and acid suppression washout. Case 2. A patient failed PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin, then reports taking bismuth + tetracycline + metronidazole + PPI (“quadruple therapy”) but only received 7 days and missed many afternoon doses. Answer: first verify whether truly optimized BQT was completed; do not assume multidrug resistance from regimen names alone. Case 3. Two fully documented regimens failed and stool PCR predicts clarithromycin resistance. Answer: do not use clarithromycin; consider susceptibility-directed management, including dedicated EGD biopsy culture if needed, after reviewing adherence and prior drug exposure.
